docs.title: Pydantic Handbook
docs.text:
A practical, example-driven guide to Pydantic v2, the most widely used data validation library for Python.

Pydantic turns Python type hints into runtime validation, parsing and serialization. It powers FastAPI and the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs, as well as LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI and PydanticAI. That makes it a core skill for backend and AI engineering roles.

Versions

Written and tested against Pydantic 2.13 and pydantic-settings 2.16 on Python 3.11+. Every code example on this site is executed in CI.

docs.title: 60-Second Example
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError


class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str = Field(min_length=1)
    email: str
    tags: list[str] = []


user = User.model_validate({"id": "42", "name": "Lenin", "email": "lenin@example.com"})
print(user.id)            # 42  (coerced from "42")
print(user.model_dump())  # {'id': 42, 'name': 'Lenin', 'email': 'lenin@example.com', 'tags': []}

try:
    User(id="abc", name="", email="x")
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e.error_count())  # 2

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
Aliases bridge naming conventions — e.g. camelCase JSON to snake_case Python.

from pydantic import AliasChoices, AliasPath, BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field
from pydantic.alias_generators import to_camel


class GitHubUser(BaseModel):
    login: str
    avatar: str = Field(alias="avatar_url")                                  # one external name
    full_name: str = Field(validation_alias=AliasChoices("name", "fullName"))  # accept several
    city: str = Field(validation_alias=AliasPath("location", "city"))       # pull from nested path


u = GitHubUser.model_validate({
    "login": "leninjoseph",
    "avatar_url": "https://x/y.png",
    "fullName": "Lenin Joseph",
    "location": {"city": "Chennai"},
})
print(u.full_name, u.city)


class CamelModel(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(alias_generator=to_camel, populate_by_name=True)

    first_name: str
    last_name: str


m = CamelModel.model_validate({"firstName": "Lenin", "lastName": "Joseph"})
print(m.model_dump(by_alias=True))   # {'firstName': 'Lenin', 'lastName': 'Joseph'}
CamelModel(first_name="A", last_name="B")   # works because populate_by_name=True
  • alias — used for both validation and serialization.
  • validation_alias — input only.
  • serialization_alias — output only (needs by_alias=True).

docs.title: Annotated Types and Reusable Constraints
docs.text:
typing.Annotated lets you package a type plus its constraints and validators into a reusable alias.

from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import AfterValidator, BaseModel, BeforeValidator, Field, StringConstraints

Username = Annotated[str, StringConstraints(strip_whitespace=True, to_lower=True, min_length=3, max_length=30)]
Percentage = Annotated[float, Field(ge=0, le=100)]


def must_be_even(v: int) -> int:
    if v % 2:
        raise ValueError("must be even")
    return v


EvenInt = Annotated[int, AfterValidator(must_be_even)]
CommaList = Annotated[list[str], BeforeValidator(lambda v: v.split(",") if isinstance(v, str) else v)]


class Profile(BaseModel):
    username: Username
    completion: Percentage
    lucky_number: EvenInt
    skills: CommaList


print(Profile(username="  LENIN ", completion=87.5, lucky_number=4, skills="python,ai,fastapi"))
# username='lenin' completion=87.5 lucky_number=4 skills=['python', 'ai', 'fastapi']

This is the cleanest way to share validation logic across many models — far better than copy-pasting @field_validators.

docs.title: Computed Fields
docs.text:
@computed_field exposes a property in serialization and JSON Schema.

from pydantic import BaseModel, computed_field


class Rectangle(BaseModel):
    width: float
    height: float

    @computed_field
    @property
    def area(self) -> float:
        return self.width * self.height


r = Rectangle(width=3, height=4)
print(r.model_dump())   # {'width': 3.0, 'height': 4.0, 'area': 12.0}

Computed fields are output-only — they're ignored if passed as input.

docs.title: Pydantic dataclasses
docs.text:
If you prefer the dataclass style:

from pydantic.dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int = 0


print(Point(x="5"))   # Point(x=5, y=0)

They validate on init but don't have model_dump etc.; use TypeAdapter(Point).dump_python(p) to serialize.

docs.title: TypedDict
docs.text:
Validate plain dicts while keeping them as dicts:

from typing_extensions import NotRequired, TypedDict  # use typing_extensions on Python < 3.12
from pydantic import TypeAdapter


class MovieDict(TypedDict):
    title: str
    year: int
    rating: NotRequired[float]


movie = TypeAdapter(MovieDict).validate_python({"title": "Arrival", "year": "2016"})
print(movie, type(movie))   # {'title': 'Arrival', 'year': 2016} <class 'dict'>

docs.title: Which to choose?
docs.text: Use When BaseModel Default choice. Richest API (dump, copy, schema, config). @pydantic.dataclasses.dataclass You want dataclass semantics or are adding validation to existing dataclasses. TypedDict + TypeAdapter You need plain dicts (e.g. passing to libraries expecting dicts), or zero object overhead.

docs.title: Generic Models
docs.text:
from typing import Generic, TypeVar
from pydantic import BaseModel

T = TypeVar("T")


class Page(BaseModel, Generic[T]):
    items: list[T]
    total: int
    page: int = 1
    size: int = 20


class Article(BaseModel):
    title: str


page = Page[Article].model_validate({"items": [{"title": "Hello"}], "total": 1})
print(page.items[0].title)   # Hello

On Python 3.12+ you can use the new syntax: class Page[T](BaseModel): ....

Great for API envelopes: ApiResponse[T], Page[T], Result[T].

docs.title: Model Configuration (ConfigDict)
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict


class StrictApiModel(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(
        extra="forbid",              # "ignore" (default) | "allow" | "forbid"
        frozen=True,                 # immutable + hashable
        str_strip_whitespace=True,
        str_min_length=1,
        validate_assignment=True,    # re-validate on attribute assignment
        validate_default=True,       # validate default values too
        use_enum_values=True,        # store enum .value instead of the member
        from_attributes=True,        # allow model_validate(orm_obj)
        populate_by_name=True,
    )

The settings you'll use most:

Option Why extra="forbid" Catch typos in client payloads ("emial" raises instead of being silently dropped). frozen=True Value objects, cache keys, safe sharing across threads. validate_assignment=True Keep the object valid after mutation. from_attributes=True Build models from ORM objects (SQLAlchemy) or any object with attributes. 
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict


class UserOut(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)
    id: int
    name: str


class FakeOrmRow:
    def __init__(self):
        self.id = 7
        self.name = "Lenin"
        self.password_hash = "secret"   # not in the model -> not exposed


print(UserOut.model_validate(FakeOrmRow()))   # id=7 name='Lenin'

Config is inherited — define a project BaseSchema once and subclass it everywhere.

docs.title: Serialization: model_dump and model_dump_json
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Event(BaseModel):
    id: int
    title: str
    notes: str | None = None
    internal_score: float = Field(default=0.0, exclude=True)
    created: datetime


e = Event(id=1, title="Launch", created="2026-11-05T12:00:00")

e.model_dump()                       # Python objects (datetime stays datetime)
e.model_dump(mode="json")            # JSON-safe types (datetime -> str)
e.model_dump_json(indent=2)          # JSON string
e.model_dump(include={"id", "title"})
e.model_dump(exclude={"notes"})
e.model_dump(exclude_none=True)      # drop None values
e.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)     # only fields explicitly provided
e.model_dump(exclude_defaults=True)  # drop fields equal to their default
e.model_dump(by_alias=True)          # use aliases as keys

exclude_unset=True is the idiomatic way to implement PATCH endpoints:

from pydantic import BaseModel


class UserUpdate(BaseModel):
    name: str | None = None
    email: str | None = None


patch = UserUpdate(email="new@example.com")
print(patch.model_dump(exclude_unset=True))   # {'email': 'new@example.com'}

docs.title: Copying with changes
docs.text:
updated = e.model_copy(update={"title": "Relaunch"})

model_copy(update=...) does not validate the update — validate first if the data is untrusted.

docs.title: Custom serializers
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime
from decimal import Decimal
from typing import Any
from pydantic import BaseModel, field_serializer, model_serializer


class Invoice(BaseModel):
    amount: Decimal
    issued: datetime

    @field_serializer("amount")
    def amount_as_str(self, v: Decimal) -> str:
        return f"{v:.2f}"

    @field_serializer("issued")
    def issued_as_date(self, v: datetime) -> str:
        return v.date().isoformat()


print(Invoice(amount="10.5", issued="2026-11-05T09:00:00").model_dump_json())
# {"amount":"10.50","issued":"2026-11-05"}


class Envelope(BaseModel):
    payload: dict[str, Any]

    @model_serializer(mode="wrap")
    def add_version(self, handler) -> dict[str, Any]:
        data = handler(self)
        data["api_version"] = "v1"
        return data

docs.title: TypeAdapter: Validating Without a Model
docs.text:
TypeAdapter brings full Pydantic validation to any type — lists, dicts, unions, TypedDicts — without defining a BaseModel.

from pydantic import BaseModel, TypeAdapter


class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str


users_adapter = TypeAdapter(list[User])
users = users_adapter.validate_json('[{"id": 1, "name": "A"}, {"id": "2", "name": "B"}]')
print(users_adapter.dump_json(users))

int_map = TypeAdapter(dict[str, int])
print(int_map.validate_python({"a": "1", "b": 2}))   # {'a': 1, 'b': 2}
print(int_map.json_schema())

Create adapters once at module level — building one is relatively expensive; using it is cheap.

docs.title: Plain unions
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel


class Item(BaseModel):
    value: int | str


print(Item(value=1).value)     # 1
print(Item(value="1").value)   # '1'  (smart mode keeps exact type matches)

Pydantic's "smart" union mode first looks for an exact type match before trying coercion.

docs.title: Discriminated (tagged) unions
docs.text:
When each variant has a literal "type" field, tell Pydantic about it. Validation becomes faster, and error messages point at the correct variant instead of listing failures for every option.

from typing import Annotated, Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, TypeAdapter


class Cat(BaseModel):
    pet_type: Literal["cat"]
    meows: int


class Dog(BaseModel):
    pet_type: Literal["dog"]
    barks: float


class Lizard(BaseModel):
    pet_type: Literal["lizard"]
    scales: bool


Pet = Annotated[Cat | Dog | Lizard, Field(discriminator="pet_type")]


class Owner(BaseModel):
    pets: list[Pet]


o = Owner.model_validate({"pets": [{"pet_type": "dog", "barks": 3}, {"pet_type": "cat", "meows": 1}]})
print([type(p).__name__ for p in o.pets])   # ['Dog', 'Cat']

pet = TypeAdapter(Pet).validate_python({"pet_type": "lizard", "scales": True})

This pattern is essential for event systems, webhook payloads and LLM tool calls (see LLM Structured Outputs).

docs.title: @validate_call: Validating Function Arguments
docs.text:
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import Field, ValidationError, validate_call


@validate_call
def repeat(text: str, times: Annotated[int, Field(gt=0, le=10)]) -> str:
    return text * times


print(repeat("ab", "3"))   # ababab  ("3" coerced to 3)

try:
    repeat("ab", 50)
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e.errors()[0]["msg"])   # Input should be less than or equal to 10

Add @validate_call(validate_return=True) to also validate the return value. Useful for public library functions and for the tool functions you expose to an LLM agent.

docs.title: Field validators
docs.text:
@field_validator runs on one or more specific fields. It must be a @classmethod.

from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator


class Signup(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: str

    @field_validator("username")
    @classmethod
    def username_alphanumeric(cls, v: str) -> str:
        if not v.isalnum():
            raise ValueError("must be alphanumeric")
        return v.lower()            # validators can also transform

    @field_validator("username", "email")
    @classmethod
    def strip_whitespace(cls, v: str) -> str:
        return v.strip()

Raise ValueError or AssertionError; Pydantic wraps them into a ValidationError.

docs.title: Validator modes
Model validators (cross-field checks)
docs.text:
from datetime import date
from typing import Self
from pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator


class Booking(BaseModel):
    check_in: date
    check_out: date
    password: str
    password_confirm: str

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def check_dates_and_passwords(self) -> Self:
        if self.check_out <= self.check_in:
            raise ValueError("check_out must be after check_in")
        if self.password != self.password_confirm:
            raise ValueError("passwords do not match")
        return self

typing.Self needs Python 3.11+. On 3.10 use from typing_extensions import Self.

A mode="before" model validator receives the raw input (usually a dict) — useful for renaming legacy keys or unwrapping envelopes:

from typing import Any
from pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator


class ApiResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str

    @model_validator(mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def unwrap(cls, data: Any) -> Any:
        if isinstance(data, dict) and "data" in data:
            return data["data"]
        return data


print(ApiResponse.model_validate({"data": {"id": 1, "name": "x"}}))

docs.title: Validation context
docs.text:
Pass runtime information (current user, allowed values from a DB) into validators:

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationInfo, field_validator


class Doc(BaseModel):
    category: str

    @field_validator("category")
    @classmethod
    def check_allowed(cls, v: str, info: ValidationInfo) -> str:
        allowed = (info.context or {}).get("allowed_categories")
        if allowed is not None and v not in allowed:
            raise ValueError(f"category must be one of {allowed}")
        return v


Doc.model_validate({"category": "ai"}, context={"allowed_categories": {"ai", "ml"}})

docs.title: Pydantic for LLM and AI Engineering
docs.text: LLM output is the definition of untrusted input. Pydantic is the de facto standard for structured outputs across the AI ecosystem — the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs, LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, Instructor and PydanticAI all build on it.

docs.title: Define the output contract
docs.text:
from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class ExtractedJob(BaseModel):
    """Structured information extracted from a job posting."""

    title: str = Field(description="Job title as written in the posting")
    company: str
    country: str = Field(description="ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code, e.g. 'DE', 'NL'")
    remote: Literal["onsite", "hybrid", "remote"]
    salary_min_eur: int | None = Field(default=None, ge=0, description="Annual minimum in EUR, if stated")
    skills: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list, max_length=20)
    visa_sponsorship: bool | None = Field(default=None, description="null if the posting does not say")

Descriptions matter: they become part of the schema the model sees, so write them as instructions.

docs.title: Validate-and-retry loop
docs.text:
from pydantic import ValidationError


def call_llm(prompt: str) -> str:
    """Placeholder for your LLM client call returning raw JSON text."""
    return '{"title": "AI Engineer", "company": "Acme", "country": "NL", "remote": "hybrid", "skills": ["python"]}'


def extract_job(posting: str, max_retries: int = 2) -> ExtractedJob:
    schema = ExtractedJob.model_json_schema()
    prompt = f"Extract the job as JSON matching this schema:\n{schema}\n\nPosting:\n{posting}"

    for attempt in range(max_retries + 1):
        raw = call_llm(prompt)
        try:
            return ExtractedJob.model_validate_json(raw)
        except ValidationError as e:
            if attempt == max_retries:
                raise
            # Feed the precise errors back so the model can self-correct
            prompt += f"\n\nYour previous answer was invalid:\n{e.json()}\nReturn corrected JSON only."
    raise RuntimeError("unreachable")


print(extract_job("We're hiring an AI Engineer in Amsterdam..."))

docs.title: Tool calling with discriminated unions
docs.text:
Model every tool's arguments as a variant, and route the LLM's choice safely:

from typing import Annotated, Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, TypeAdapter


class WebSearch(BaseModel):
    tool: Literal["web_search"]
    query: str


class GetWeather(BaseModel):
    tool: Literal["get_weather"]
    city: str
    unit: Literal["c", "f"] = "c"


class SendEmail(BaseModel):
    tool: Literal["send_email"]
    to: str
    subject: str
    body: str


ToolCall = Annotated[WebSearch | GetWeather | SendEmail, Field(discriminator="tool")]
tool_adapter = TypeAdapter(ToolCall)


def dispatch(raw_json: str) -> str:
    call = tool_adapter.validate_json(raw_json)
    match call:
        case WebSearch(query=q):
            return f"searching for {q!r}"
        case GetWeather(city=c, unit=u):
            return f"weather in {c} ({u})"
        case SendEmail():
            return "email requires human confirmation"   # gate side effects!


print(dispatch('{"tool": "get_weather", "city": "Berlin"}'))

Generate the tool definitions straight from the models:

tools = [
    {
        "name": m.model_fields["tool"].annotation.__args__[0],
        "description": m.__doc__ or "",
        "input_schema": m.model_json_schema(),
    }
    for m in (WebSearch, GetWeather, SendEmail)
]

docs.title: With the Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs
docs.text:
Both SDKs accept Pydantic models directly for structured outputs; check the current docs for the exact method names, as these APIs evolve quickly. The general shape:

# OpenAI (sketch)
# completion = client.chat.completions.parse(model=..., messages=..., response_format=ExtractedJob)
# job = completion.choices[0].message.parsed

# Anthropic (sketch) — pass ExtractedJob.model_json_schema() as a tool's input_schema,
# then validate the returned tool_use input:

docs.title: RAG and agent state
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Chunk(BaseModel):
    id: str
    text: str
    source: str
    page: int | None = None
    score: float = Field(ge=0, le=1)


class RetrievalResult(BaseModel):
    query: str
    chunks: list[Chunk]
    retrieved_at: datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.now)

    def as_context(self, max_chars: int = 4000) -> str:
        out, used = [], 0
        for c in sorted(self.chunks, key=lambda c: c.score, reverse=True):
            block = f"[{c.source} p.{c.page}] {c.text}"
            if used + len(block) > max_chars:
                break
            out.append(block)
            used += len(block)
        return "\n\n".join(out)


class AgentState(BaseModel):
    goal: str
    steps_taken: list[str] = []
    scratchpad: dict[str, str] = {}
    done: bool = False

Typed state makes agents easier to checkpoint (model_dump_json), resume (model_validate_json) and debug.

docs.title: AI-specific tips
docs.text:
• Make "unknown" representable. Use X | None with a description like "null if not stated" — otherwise the model is pressured to hallucinate a value.
  • Use Literal / Enum for categories so the model can't invent new labels.
  • Keep schemas shallow and small. Deeply nested, huge schemas degrade output quality.
  • Validate business rules with validators (e.g. salary_max >= salary_min) — the model will occasionally get them wrong.
  • Never trust tool arguments for side effects. Validate, then authorize, then execute.

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text: Use Pydantic at the boundaries of your system: HTTP requests, config files, environment variables, queues and LLM outputs. Anywhere untrusted data enters, describe its shape with a model and let Pydantic enforce it.

docs.title: Fields: Types, Defaults and Constraints
docs.text:
Use Field() to attach defaults, constraints and metadata.

from uuid import UUID, uuid4
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Product(BaseModel):
    id: UUID = Field(default_factory=uuid4)
    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=100)
    price: float = Field(gt=0, description="Price in EUR")
    quantity: int = Field(default=0, ge=0)
    sku: str = Field(pattern=r"^[A-Z]{3}-\d{4}$")
    discount: float = Field(default=0.0, ge=0, le=1)


p = Product(name="Keyboard", price=49.99, sku="KEY-0001")
print(p)

docs.title: Common Field arguments
docs.text: Argument Applies to Meaning default / default_factory any static default / callable producing a default gt, ge, lt, le numbers >, >=, <, <= multiple_of numbers value must be a multiple min_length, max_length str, list, set, dict size bounds pattern str regex the string must match alias any external name for the field description, examples, title any documentation; flows into JSON Schema exclude any omit from serialization frozen any field cannot be reassigned repr any hide from repr() (e.g. secrets)

docs.title: Useful built-in types
docs.text:
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, HttpUrl, SecretStr, PositiveInt


class Account(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr           # needs pydantic[email]
    website: HttpUrl
    password: SecretStr       # hidden in repr and dumps
    balance: Decimal
    age: PositiveInt
    birthday: date


acc = Account(
    email="lenin@example.com",
    website="https://example.com",
    password="hunter2",
    balance="1024.50",
    age=31,
    birthday="1994-03-22",
)
print(acc.password)                     # **********
print(acc.password.get_secret_value())  # hunter2

docs.title: Your First Model
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime
from pydantic import BaseModel


class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str
    signup_ts: datetime | None = None
    tags: list[str] = []


user = User(id="123", name="Lenin", signup_ts="2026-01-15T10:30:00")

print(user.id)          # 123  (str "123" coerced to int)
print(user.signup_ts)   # 2026-01-15 10:30:00  (str parsed into datetime)
print(user.tags)        # []
print(user.model_dump())
# {'id': 123, 'name': 'Lenin', 'signup_ts': datetime.datetime(2026, 1, 15, 10, 30), 'tags': []}

Key points:

  • Fields without a default are required.
  • X | None = None makes a field optional.
  • Mutable defaults like [] are safe — Pydantic copies them per instance (unlike plain Python classes).

docs.title: Three ways to build a model
docs.text:
User(id=1, name="A")                                 # keyword args
User.model_validate({"id": 1, "name": "A"})          # from a dict
User.model_validate_json('{"id": 1, "name": "A"}')   # from a JSON string (fastest path)

Prefer model_validate_json when you already have raw JSON — it parses and validates in one Rust pass instead of json.loads + validate.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install pydantic                 # core library
pip install "pydantic[email]"        # adds EmailStr support
pip install pydantic-settings        # settings / env var management

Check the version:

import pydantic
print(pydantic.VERSION)

docs.title: What Pydantic Is (and Isn't)
docs.text:
Pydantic is a data validation and parsing library driven by Python type hints. You describe the shape of your data with ordinary annotations, and Pydantic:

  • Validates incoming data against those types and constraints.
  • Coerces compatible input into the declared type (e.g. "42" → 42) unless you ask for strict mode.
  • Serializes objects back into dicts and JSON.
  • Generates JSON Schema describing the model.

The core validation engine (pydantic-core) is written in Rust, which makes v2 dramatically faster than v1.

What Pydantic is not:

  • Not an ORM — it doesn't talk to databases (though it pairs well with SQLAlchemy and SQLModel).
  • Not a static type checker — it validates at runtime. Use mypy/pyright alongside it.
  • Not a guarantee once the object exists — by default, assigning an invalid value to an attribute after creation is not re-validated (see validate_assignment).

Rule of thumb: use Pydantic at the boundaries of your system — HTTP requests, config files, environment variables, message queues, LLM outputs — anywhere untrusted data enters.

docs.title: Nested Models and Collections
docs.text:
Models compose naturally. Validation recurses through nested models, lists, dicts and tuples.

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Address(BaseModel):
    street: str
    city: str
    country: str = "NL"


class LineItem(BaseModel):
    sku: str
    qty: int
    unit_price: float


class Customer(BaseModel):
    name: str
    address: Address
    items: list[LineItem]
    metadata: dict[str, str] = {}
    coordinates: tuple[float, float] | None = None


c = Customer.model_validate({
    "name": "Lenin",
    "address": {"street": "Damrak 1", "city": "Amsterdam"},
    "items": [
        {"sku": "A1", "qty": "2", "unit_price": "9.99"},
        {"sku": "B2", "qty": 1, "unit_price": 20},
    ],
    "coordinates": [52.37, 4.89],
})

print(c.address.city)        # Amsterdam
print(c.items[0].qty)        # 2
print(c.coordinates)         # (52.37, 4.89)

Errors in nested data point to the exact location, e.g. ('items', 1, 'qty').

docs.title: Self-referencing models
docs.text:
from __future__ import annotations
from pydantic import BaseModel


class TreeNode(BaseModel):
    value: int
    children: list[TreeNode] = []


tree = TreeNode(value=1, children=[{"value": 2}, {"value": 3, "children": [{"value": 4}]}])
print(tree.children[1].children[0].value)  # 4

docs.title: Strict vs Lax Mode
docs.text:
By default Pydantic runs in lax mode: it coerces sensible inputs ("42" → 42, "true" → True). Strict mode refuses any type conversion.

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, StrictInt, ValidationError


class Lax(BaseModel):
    count: int


class Strict(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True)
    count: int


class Mixed(BaseModel):
    count: StrictInt               # strict on this field only
    ratio: float = Field(strict=False)


print(Lax(count="42").count)       # 42

try:
    Strict(count="42")
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e.errors()[0]["type"])   # int_type

You can also opt in per call: Lax.model_validate(data, strict=True).

When to use strict mode: internal service-to-service contracts and financial data where silent coercion could hide bugs. Keep lax mode for user-facing inputs like query strings and form data, which always arrive as strings.

Note: when validating JSON with model_validate_json, strict mode still allows types that JSON can't express natively — e.g. ISO strings for datetime or UUID.

docs.title: Validation Errors
docs.text:
When validation fails Pydantic raises a single ValidationError that collects every problem, not just the first.

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError


class Order(BaseModel):
    order_id: int
    amount: float = Field(gt=0)
    currency: str = Field(min_length=3, max_length=3)


try:
    Order(order_id="abc", amount=-5, currency="EURO")
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e.error_count())  # 3
    for err in e.errors():
        print(err["loc"], err["type"], "-", err["msg"])

Output:

('order_id',) int_parsing - Input should be a valid integer, unable to parse string as an integer
('amount',) greater_than - Input should be greater than 0
('currency',) string_too_long - String should have at most 3 characters

Each error dict contains:

  • loc — path to the failing field (tuples like ('items', 2, 'price') for nested data)
  • type — a stable machine-readable error code (good for i18n or API error mapping)
  • msg — human-readable message
  • input — the value that failed

e.json() gives the same as a JSON string — handy for API responses.

docs.title: Pydantic Interview Questions
docs.text: Common questions asked in Python backend and AI engineering interviews. Each answer is short enough to say out loud. Answers start collapsed, so you can test yourself first.

docs.title: Fundamentals
Validation
docs.text:
7. What are the four validator modes? Mode When it runs Typical use after (default) After Pydantic's type validation Business rules on typed values before Before type validation, on the raw input Normalising messy input (e.g. CSV → list) wrap Around Pydantic's validation, with a handler Fallbacks, logging, catching errors plain Instead of Pydantic's validation Fully custom parsing 8. field_validator vs model_validator: when do you use each?

Use @field_validator for rules about a single field, such as "username is alphanumeric". Use @model_validator(mode="after") for cross-field rules, such as "end_date is after start_date" or "the two passwords match". A mode="before" model validator can reshape the raw input before any field is validated.

9. How do you pass runtime data (like the current user or allowed values) into a validator?

Use validation context. Call Model.model_validate(data, context={...}) and read info.context inside a validator that accepts info: ValidationInfo. That way validators never need globals or database calls.

10. Is an attribute re-validated when I assign to it after creation?

Not by default. Set ConfigDict(validate_assignment=True) to re-validate on assignment, or frozen=True to make the model immutable.

11. What does a ValidationError contain?

It contains every error, not just the first. Each entry in e.errors() has these keys:

  • loc: the path to the failing field, e.g. ('items', 2, 'price')
  • type: a stable error code, e.g. greater_than
  • msg: a human-readable message
  • input: the value that failed

e.json() gives the same as JSON, which is handy for API error responses.

12. How do you reuse the same constraint across many models?

Define an Annotated alias once and use it everywhere:

from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, StringConstraints

Username = Annotated[str, StringConstraints(strip_whitespace=True, to_lower=True, min_length=3)]
Percentage = Annotated[float, Field(ge=0, le=100)]


class Profile(BaseModel):
    username: Username
    completion: Percentage

docs.title: Serialization & Config
docs.text:
13. What's the difference between model_dump() and model_dump(mode='json')?

model_dump() returns Python objects, so a datetime stays a datetime. mode="json" returns only JSON-compatible types, so a datetime becomes an ISO string and a UUID becomes a string. model_dump_json() goes straight to a JSON string and is faster.

14. How would you implement a PATCH endpoint with Pydantic?

Make every field optional, then use model_dump(exclude_unset=True). That returns only the fields the client actually sent, so None values the client didn't send never overwrite stored data.

15. What does extra='forbid' do, and why use it?

It makes unknown keys raise an error instead of being silently ignored (the default). For request bodies, this turns client typos like "emial" into a clear 422 instead of a silent data bug.

16. How do you convert between camelCase JSON and snake_case Python?

Set ConfigDict(alias_generator=to_camel, populate_by_name=True), using pydantic.alias_generators.to_camel. Input then accepts camelCase, and model_dump(by_alias=True) outputs camelCase. With populate_by_name=True, Python code can still use the snake_case names.

17. How do you build a Pydantic model from an ORM object?

Set ConfigDict(from_attributes=True), then call Model.model_validate(orm_obj). Pydantic reads the object's attributes. Only fields declared on the model are included, which keeps columns like password_hash out of responses.

18. How do you keep secrets out of logs?

Use the SecretStr type. It shows as ********** in repr, str and dumps, and you read the real value with .get_secret_value(). Alternatively, use Field(repr=False, exclude=True).

docs.title: Advanced Types
docs.text:
19. What is a discriminated union and why is it better than a plain union?

It's a union where every variant has a Literal "tag" field, such as type: Literal["cat"]. You declare it with Field(discriminator="type"). Pydantic reads the tag and validates against the one matching variant. This is faster than trying each variant, and the errors refer only to that variant. It's the standard pattern for webhooks, event streams and LLM tool calls.

20. What is TypeAdapter for?

It runs Pydantic validation and serialization on any type that isn't a BaseModel, such as list[User], dict[str, int], unions or TypedDicts. You create it once and reuse it: TypeAdapter(list[User]).validate_json(raw). It replaces v1's parse_obj_as.

21. When would you choose TypedDict or a Pydantic dataclass over BaseModel?
  • BaseModel is the default, with the richest API: dump, copy, schema and config.
  • Pydantic dataclass: you want dataclass semantics, or you're adding validation to existing dataclasses.
  • TypedDict + TypeAdapter: you need the result to stay a plain dict, or you want minimal overhead.
22. What does model_construct() do and when is it dangerous?

It creates an instance without any validation, which is fast. It's only safe for data you already trust, such as data you just produced yourself. Using it on external input defeats the purpose of Pydantic.

docs.title: Settings, FastAPI & Performance
docs.text:
23. How does pydantic-settings resolve a value?

In priority order: init kwargs, then environment variables, then the .env file, then the secrets directory, then field defaults. env_prefix namespaces the variables (e.g. APP_). env_nested_delimiter="__" maps APP_DB__POOL_SIZE to settings.db.pool_size. Wrap the settings in @lru_cache so they're loaded once.

24. Why have separate UserCreate, UserUpdate and UserOut schemas in FastAPI?

Each direction has different rules:

  • Create accepts a password.
  • Update makes every field optional, for PATCH.
  • Out must never expose the password and adds server fields like id and created_at.

One shared model either leaks data or forces awkward optionality. FastAPI's response_model also filters the output to the declared schema.

25. How do you make Pydantic validation faster?
  • Use model_validate_json on raw JSON instead of json.loads followed by validation.
  • Build each TypeAdapter once, at module level.
  • Prefer discriminated unions to plain unions.
  • Prefer declarative constraints (Field(gt=0)), which run in Rust, over Python validators.
  • Avoid wrap validators on hot paths.
  • Use model_construct only for trusted data.

docs.title: AI Engineering
docs.text:
26. How would you get reliable structured output from an LLM?
  1. Define a Pydantic model as the output contract, with a description on each field. The descriptions become instructions in the schema.
  2. Pass model_json_schema() to the LLM as a tool schema or response format.
  3. Validate the response with model_validate_json.
  4. On a ValidationError, send e.json() back to the model and retry a bounded number of times.
  5. Enforce business rules with validators, because the model will sometimes violate them.
27. How do you design schemas so LLMs hallucinate less?
  • Make "unknown" representable: use X | None with a description like "null if not stated".
  • Use Literal or Enum for categories so the model can't invent labels.
  • Keep schemas small and shallow.
  • Write field descriptions as instructions to the model.
28. How would you safely route LLM tool calls?

Model each tool's arguments as one variant of a discriminated union keyed on the tool name, and validate with a TypeAdapter. Then dispatch with match. Validation only proves the arguments are well-formed, not that the action is allowed. Authorize before any side effect, and require human confirmation for destructive actions like sending email or making payments.

Practice

For every question, try writing the code from memory, then compare it with the relevant page in this handbook.

docs.text:

docs.title: Pydantic with FastAPI
docs.text:
FastAPI uses Pydantic for request bodies, query params, responses and docs. A clean pattern is separate schemas per direction:

from datetime import datetime
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, EmailStr, Field

app = FastAPI()


class UserBase(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")
    email: EmailStr
    full_name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=100)


class UserCreate(UserBase):
    password: str = Field(min_length=8)


class UserUpdate(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr | None = None
    full_name: str | None = None


class UserOut(UserBase):
    model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)
    id: int
    created_at: datetime


DB: dict[int, dict] = {}


@app.post("/users", response_model=UserOut, status_code=201)
def create_user(payload: UserCreate) -> UserOut:
    user_id = len(DB) + 1
    record = {**payload.model_dump(exclude={"password"}), "id": user_id, "created_at": datetime.now()}
    DB[user_id] = record
    return UserOut.model_validate(record)


@app.patch("/users/{user_id}", response_model=UserOut)
def update_user(user_id: int, patch: UserUpdate) -> UserOut:
    if user_id not in DB:
        raise HTTPException(404, "User not found")
    DB[user_id].update(patch.model_dump(exclude_unset=True))
    return UserOut.model_validate(DB[user_id])

Why this works:

  • UserCreate accepts the password; UserOut can never leak it.
  • response_model filters the output even if you accidentally return extra fields.
  • extra="forbid" turns client typos into clear 422 errors.
  • exclude_unset=True makes PATCH update only what the client sent.

docs.title: JSON Schema Generation
docs.text:
import json
from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class SearchQuery(BaseModel):
    """Search the knowledge base."""

    query: str = Field(description="Natural-language search query", examples=["pydantic validators"])
    top_k: int = Field(default=5, ge=1, le=50)
    mode: Literal["semantic", "keyword", "hybrid"] = "hybrid"


print(json.dumps(SearchQuery.model_json_schema(), indent=2))

The class docstring becomes the schema description, and every Field(description=...) lands on its property. These schemas power:

  • FastAPI's OpenAPI / Swagger docs
  • LLM function/tool calling definitions
  • Frontend form generation and contract tests

Use model_json_schema(mode="serialization") to describe the output shape (includes computed fields, respects serialization aliases).

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Use model_validate_json on raw JSON instead of json.loads + model_validate.
  2. Reuse TypeAdapters — create them once at import time.
  3. Prefer discriminated unions over plain unions with many members.
  4. Prefer Annotated constraints (Field(gt=0)) over Python validators — constraints run in Rust.
  5. Avoid mode="wrap" validators on hot paths; they're the slowest kind.
  6. Use model_construct() to skip validation for data you already trust (e.g. rows you just wrote yourself):
from pydantic import BaseModel


class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str


fast = User.model_construct(id=1, name="trusted")   # no validation at all!
  1. Use TypedDict instead of nested models when you don't need model instances.
  2. Choose list / dict over abstract Sequence / Mapping where possible — concrete types validate faster.

docs.title: Settings Management with pydantic-settings
docs.text:
BaseSettings reads values from environment variables, .env files and secrets directories, then validates them like any model.

from pydantic import Field, SecretStr, PostgresDsn
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict


class DatabaseSettings(BaseSettings):
    url: PostgresDsn = "postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/app"
    pool_size: int = 5


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
        env_file=".env",
        env_file_encoding="utf-8",
        env_prefix="APP_",            # APP_DEBUG, APP_OPENAI_API_KEY, ...
        env_nested_delimiter="__",    # APP_DB__POOL_SIZE=10
        extra="ignore",
    )

    debug: bool = False
    environment: str = "dev"
    openai_api_key: SecretStr = SecretStr("")
    allowed_origins: list[str] = ["http://localhost:3000"]   # set as JSON: '["https://a.com"]'
    db: DatabaseSettings = Field(default_factory=DatabaseSettings)


settings = Settings()

.env example:

APP_DEBUG=true
APP_ENVIRONMENT=prod
APP_OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
APP_DB__POOL_SIZE=20
APP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=["https://app.example.com"]

Priority order (highest wins): init kwargs → environment variables → .env file → secrets dir → field defaults.

docs.title: Cache it
docs.text:
from functools import lru_cache


@lru_cache
def get_settings() -> Settings:
    return Settings()

In FastAPI, inject it with Depends(get_settings); in tests, override the dependency or call get_settings.cache_clear().

Best practices

  • Wrap every secret in SecretStr so it never shows up in logs or tracebacks.
  • Fail fast: instantiate settings at startup so misconfiguration crashes the deploy, not the first request.
  • Commit a .env.example, never .env.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
from typing import Annotated, Literal
from pydantic import (
    BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, TypeAdapter, ValidationError,
    field_validator, model_validator, computed_field,
    field_serializer, validate_call, SecretStr, EmailStr, HttpUrl,
)

# ---- Define
class M(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", str_strip_whitespace=True)
    a: int = Field(gt=0)
    b: str | None = None
    c: list[str] = []
    kind: Literal["x", "y"] = "x"

# ---- Create
M(a=1)
M.model_validate({"a": 1})
M.model_validate_json('{"a": 1}')
M.model_construct(a=1)            # no validation

# ---- Export
m = M(a=1)
m.model_dump()
m.model_dump(mode="json", exclude_none=True, by_alias=True)
m.model_dump_json(indent=2)
m.model_copy(update={"a": 2})
M.model_json_schema()

# ---- Introspect
M.model_fields                     # dict of FieldInfo
m.model_fields_set                 # fields explicitly set

# ---- Validate anything
TypeAdapter(list[int]).validate_python(["1", 2])

# ---- Errors
try:
    M(a=-1)
except ValidationError as e:
    e.errors(); e.json(); e.error_count()

docs.title: 1. Assuming mutation is validated
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel


class A(BaseModel):
    n: int


a = A(n=1)
a.n = "not an int"   # no error! Use validate_assignment=True to catch this

docs.title: 2. Optional without a default
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel


class B(BaseModel):
    x: int | None        # REQUIRED (may be None)
    y: int | None = None # truly optional

docs.title: 3. Silently dropped extra fields
docs.text: The default extra="ignore" means a misspelt key just disappears. Use extra="forbid" for request bodies.

docs.title: 4. model_copy(update=...) skips validation
docs.text: Validate the merged data instead: A.model_validate({**a.model_dump(), **changes}).

docs.title: 5. model_construct() on untrusted data
docs.text: It bypasses all checks. Only use it for data you produced yourself.

docs.title: 6. Leaking secrets
docs.text: Plain str passwords show up in logs and repr. Use SecretStr, or Field(repr=False, exclude=True).

docs.title: 7. Forgetting @classmethod on validators
docs.text: v2 requires it for @field_validator and mode="before" / "wrap" model validators.

docs.title: 8. Field names shadowing BaseModel attributes
docs.text: Avoid naming fields model_*, dict, json, copy, schema. Use an alias if the external key collides.

docs.title: 9. Expensive validators doing I/O
docs.text: Don't hit the database or network inside validators. Pass precomputed data in via context.

docs.title: Migrating from v1 to v2
docs.text:
Pydantic v1 Pydantic v2 class Config: model_config = ConfigDict(...) orm_mode = True from_attributes=True allow_population_by_field_name populate_by_name .dict() .model_dump() .json() .model_dump_json() .parse_obj(d) .model_validate(d) .parse_raw(s) .model_validate_json(s) .from_orm(o) .model_validate(o) (with from_attributes) .copy(update=...) .model_copy(update=...) .schema() .model_json_schema() .construct() .model_construct() .__fields__ .model_fields @validator @field_validator @root_validator @model_validator each_item=True validate the item type with Annotated[..., AfterValidator(...)] const=True Literal[...] regex= pattern= min_items / max_items min_length / max_length parse_obj_as(T, x) TypeAdapter(T).validate_python(x) BaseSettings in pydantic BaseSettings in pydantic-settings

Behavioural changes to watch for:

  • Optional[X] without a default is now required (it just allows None). Add = None to make it optional.
  • int → str coercion is gone: passing 123 to a str field fails.
  • Validators must be @classmethods.

Use the official tool to automate most of it:

pip install bump-pydantic
bump-pydantic my_package/

from pydantic import v1 still exposes the old API if you need a gradual migration.
